title: API 510 Training in Baton Rouge: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced online API 510 exam prep for Baton Rouge, Plaquemine and Geismar vessel inspectors: columns, reactors, spheres and exchangers, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Baton Rouge: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for River Refineries, Chemical Plants and Nitrogen Complexes
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors on the Baton Rouge river corridor

Follow the Mississippi from the Baton Rouge refinery down to the nitrogen complex at Donaldsonville and you pass a heavy concentration of pressure vessels: columns, reactors, regenerators, accumulators, spheres, exchanger shells and the relief devices that protect them. This page is for plant inspection staff, contract inspectors, NDT technicians who already take the readings, and engineers who want API 510 certification behind their signature.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Baton Rouge. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions as you go, so a candidate in Baton Rouge, Port Allen, Plaquemine or Gonzales can study between shifts. The American Petroleum Institute sets the eligibility rules, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the API 510 certification. Completing the course prepares you for that examination; it is not a certification, and Atlantis holds no API approval as a training provider.

Two refineries facing each other across the Mississippi

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's refinery capacity survey, which reports the position at the start of 2026, lists two operating refineries at Baton Rouge itself: ExxonMobil Refining & Supply Co. on the east bank and Placid Refining Co. at Port Allen on the west bank. The table shows crude distillation in barrels per calendar day and, in barrels per stream day, the downstream units that hold most of each site's heavy-walled vessels.

Read each row as a family of vessels. The catalytic cracking row means a reactor, regenerator and cyclones in hot, erosive service, and at Baton Rouge it carries history: Louisiana's annual refinery report credits the refinery with the catalytic cracking technology developed there in 1942. The coking row means coke drums cycling between hot fill and water quench; the desulfurization and hydrocracking rows mean thick-walled reactors and high-pressure separators in hydrogen service. ExxonMobil says the refinery, which dates from 1909, makes about 300 products and grades.

The refinery sits inside a larger complex: a chemical plant making isopropyl alcohol and rubber for tire liners, a low-density polyethylene plant and a polyolefins plant, where a unit started in 2022 added 450,000 metric tons a year of polypropylene, plus a lubricants blending plant, with about 6,000 people in all. Across the river, Placid, an independent privately held refiner, has run Port Allen since 1975 and moved its headquarters from Dallas to Baton Rouge in 2023. The lesson for a candidate is breadth: refinery, chemical and polymer vessels within a short drive, each with its own design basis and damage picture.

Chemical plants from Plaquemine to Donaldsonville

  • Dow, Plaquemine. Dow came to Louisiana in 1956 and built Louisiana Operations, its first site in the state; it has 15 production units making more than 200 products, caustic soda, polyethylene and chlorinated polyethylene among them.
  • Shintech, Plaquemine. The PVC producer makes chlor-alkali, vinyl chloride monomer and ethylene, and announced in 2026 a second ethylene unit and a fourth chlor-alkali and vinyl chloride monomer unit.
  • BASF, Geismar. BASF calls Geismar its largest manufacturing facility in North America, with 32 production units and roughly 1,300 staff.
  • Shell, Geismar. Shell's Geismar chemical site began operating in 1967 and commissioned an additional alpha olefins unit in 2019.
  • Methanex, Geismar. Three methanol plants share one site; the newest, G3, made its first methanol in 2024.
  • CF Industries, Donaldsonville. Louisiana Economic Development describes the 1,400-acre complex as the world's largest and most flexible ammonia and nitrogen production facility, and a low-carbon ammonia joint venture with JERA and Mitsui was approved in 2025 for the west bank of Ascension Parish.

The vessels follow the chemistry: caustic evaporators in chlor-alkali, reactors and purification columns in vinyls, and hot, hydrogen-rich syngas exchangers, converters and separators in methanol and ammonia. Liquefied gas stored under pressure in spheres and bullets is vessel work under API 510. Large refrigerated ammonia storage, where a site has it, is normally built to low-pressure tank standards such as API 620 and API 625 rather than to Section VIII, a distinction worth keeping straight when you describe your experience on the API application.

What Louisiana's boiler law covers, and what falls to the owner

Revised Statutes 23:531 gives the assistant secretary of the Office of State Fire Marshal exclusive power to investigate and make rules for boilers. The rules themselves, in Title 55, Part V, Chapter 50 of the Louisiana Administrative Code, cover boilers and the inspection, during fabrication, repair or alteration, of pressure vessels that the owner or user requires to meet ASME and National Board rules and to carry the stamp. Their scope section says the rules are not designed to provide an inspection program for unfired pressure vessels, except as the act provides, although inspections are available when the owner or user asks. Evaporators and heat exchangers are excluded from jurisdictional inspection.

That leaves in-service inspection of a plant's columns, drums and reactors with the owner. Louisiana has no OSHA-approved State Plan, so federal OSHA, with an area office in Baton Rouge, enforces process safety management under 29 CFR 1910.119. Its mechanical integrity paragraph names pressure vessels and expects inspection and testing to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices. EPA's risk management program rule repeats that expectation in 40 CFR 68.73 and adds documentation requirements for every inspection. API 510 defines the authorized pressure vessel inspector and the owner-user inspection organisation that employs one, which is why plant inspection departments ask for the certification. The API 510 code guide walks through the code itself.

Damage mechanisms a corridor vessel inspector should know cold

Each window's Body of Knowledge lists the API RP 571 mechanisms examined, so read yours first. Most entries have a home somewhere between Port Allen and Donaldsonville, which makes them easier to remember.

  • Wet H2S damage and amine cracking. Refinery overheads, sour water strippers and amine regenerators.
  • Caustic stress corrosion cracking. Evaporators and caustic storage at chlor-alkali plants, where concentration, temperature and stress relief of welds decide the risk.
  • Ammonia stress corrosion cracking. Carbon steel spheres and bullets in anhydrous ammonia service, usually searched for with wet fluorescent magnetic particle testing during an internal inspection.
  • High temperature hydrogen attack. Hydroprocessing reactors and the hot syngas sections of methanol and ammonia plants.
  • Erosion and high-temperature damage. FCC reactors and regenerators, often behind refractory linings.
  • Corrosion under insulation. Insulated vessels in a climate that averages close to 62 inches of precipitation a year on NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals, plus chloride cracking of austenitic stainless steel under wet insulation.

The exam never asks which plant has which problem; it describes a mechanism, asks for the inspection method RP 571 and RP 572 associate with it, and then applies API 510's rules to what was found.

Worked example: averaging a thin area and judging scattered pits

Thickness surveys on big columns rarely show uniform loss, and API 510 has two rules for patchy results that make good exam questions.

Averaging a locally thinned area. For a corroded area of considerable size, API 510 lets wall thicknesses be averaged over a length set by the vessel's inside diameter. Up to 60 in. inside diameter, the limit is half the diameter or 20 in., whichever is less. Above 60 in., it is one third of the diameter or 40 in., whichever is less.

  • An amine regenerator of 96 in. inside diameter: one third of 96 is 32 in., which is below 40 in., so readings may be averaged over 32 in.
  • An overhead accumulator of 42 in. inside diameter: half of 42 is 21 in., but the 20 in. limit is smaller and governs.
  • A crude column of 150 in. inside diameter: one third is 50 in., so the 40 in. cap applies.

Suppose the regenerator's required thickness at the thin elevation is 0.440 in. A grid finds a lowest single reading of 0.418 in., but the average along the critical 32 in. line is 0.457 in., so on averaging the area meets the required thickness today; whether it still will after the corrosion expected before the next inspection is the follow-up question. Setting the single 0.418 in. point against 0.440 in. and rejecting the shell misses the rule being tested.

Widely scattered pits. API 510 allows widely scattered pits to be ignored when three conditions hold together: the remaining thickness below each pit is more than half the required thickness, the total area of pitting deeper than the corrosion allowance is no more than 7 sq. in. within any 8 in. diameter circle, and the sum of pit dimensions along any straight line inside that circle is no more than 2 in. With 0.440 in. required, the first condition sets a floor of 0.220 in. under every pit. A pit leaving 0.240 in. passes that test, but the area and line limits still decide whether the patch can be ignored.

Section VIII thickness, MAWP and test pressure calculations are set out on the API 510 course page.

Who sits API 510 in Baton Rouge, and the route each takes

API counts experience from the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, which includes an owner-user inspection organisation, and verifies what you document.

  • Engineers. A bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology calls for one year supervising or performing inspection activities as API 510 describes them. A graduate of LSU's ABET-accredited chemical engineering programme who joins a plant inspection group can qualify early if the role genuinely includes inspection.
  • NDT technicians. With a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology, API asks for two years of experience in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels, one of them in supervision or performance of inspection; with a high school diploma, three years on the same terms. Baton Rouge Community College's workforce NDT programme and Atlantis's ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training for Baton Rouge both lead into the readings work that builds that experience.
  • Process operators. Operating experience counts toward the total, but every route includes inspection work, so operators usually move into an inspection role first.
  • Welders and fabricators. Repair and construction experience counts too, and some take AWS CWI exam prep before API 510.
  • Military technicians. Three or more years of technical military service count like a bachelor's degree and two like a two-year degree, unless the discharge was dishonorable.

With no formal education, API asks for five or more years. The certification requirements page has the full rules.

Studying for API 510 around corridor shifts and turnarounds

Corridor plants run rotating shifts, and inspection departments add people when units come down. A self-paced course fits that rhythm: push through the calculations on days off, then drop to short sessions while a unit is open.

A sequence that works: pick the exam window from the API exam schedule and download the Publications Effectivity Sheet for it; learn API 510's own closed-book rules on intervals, repairs and rerating; drill the calculations until the formulas need no lookup; and finish with timed open-book practice in the code PDFs. When a clause reads two ways, the instructor's answer points to the paragraph it lives in, the skill the afternoon rewards.

Exam day is long. There are 170 questions, 140 of them scored and 30 unscored pretest items; 110 are closed-book and 60 open-book, across 7.5 hours that hold a short tutorial, 2.75 hours of closed-book work, a 45-minute lunch and 3.75 hours of open-book work with the code PDFs on screen. Prometric lists test centres in and around Baton Rouge, and you choose one once API has accepted your application.

Preparation options in Baton Rouge, compared fairly

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Baton Rouge plant or contractor

Owner-users and inspection contractors on the corridor can enrol several candidates together under one quote; fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API in their own name, with their own experience record and employer verification, and books a seat at a time their roster allows.

It pays to check each candidate's experience against API's rules before enrolment, to pick one target window for the group, and to pair each person with a certified inspector in the department who knows how the code is applied to that plant's vessels.

faq.q: Can I attend API 510 classes in person in Baton Rouge?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Baton Rouge. The API 510 course runs self-paced online, with instructor Q&A, so candidates in Baton Rouge, Port Allen and the Ascension Parish plants study the same material on their own schedule. The examination itself is sat in person at a Prometric test centre once API accepts your application, and API issues the certification.

faq.q: Does the Louisiana State Fire Marshal inspect refinery pressure vessels?
faq.a: Not as a routine programme. The Office of State Fire Marshal administers the boiler law, and its rules say they are not designed to provide an inspection program for unfired pressure vessels, apart from what the act provides and inspections an owner requests. In-service vessel inspection at a refinery or chemical plant is the owner's programme under OSHA process safety management, which is where API 510 inspectors come in.

faq.q: Do ammonia spheres and bullets count as API 510 experience?
faq.a: Pressurised ammonia storage designed as pressure vessels is vessel work, so inspecting it can count, provided you were supervising or performing inspection as the code describes. Large refrigerated ammonia tanks are built to tank standards instead. API verifies the application, so describe the equipment and your role plainly.

faq.q: Louisiana exempts heat exchangers from state inspection. Are they still on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Yes. The state exemption concerns jurisdictional inspection by the Fire Marshal's office, not the codes. Exchanger shells and channels are pressure vessels for API 510 purposes, and API RP 572, normally part of the Body of Knowledge, covers their inspection alongside columns, drums and reactors.

faq.q: Can an LSU chemical engineering graduate qualify for API 510 sooner than a technician?
faq.a: Usually, yes. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology shortens the experience requirement to one year of supervising or performing inspection activities, against two or three years for most technicians. The year must be real inspection work within the last 10 years for an authorized inspection agency or an owner-user inspection organisation, and API verifies it.

faq.q: I am a process operator at a Plaquemine plant. Does my experience count?
faq.a: Operating experience counts toward the total years API asks for on the two-year degree, high school and no-formal-education routes, but each of those routes also requires at least one year supervising or performing inspection. Most operators therefore move into an inspection role first. Check the API 510 requirements against your own record before you apply.

faq.q: Where do Baton Rouge candidates take the API 510 exam?
faq.a: At a Prometric test centre; Prometric lists centres in and near Baton Rouge, and you pick one after API approves your application for a window. The exam is computer-based and in person only, with no papers or books allowed in the room; for the open-book part the code PDFs are provided on screen.
